sections.title: The Mitzvot Dependent on the Land in General
sections.html:
The Torah was given to Israel so that they would study it and fulfil its mitzvot in the Land of Israel, and through this blessing would be drawn to the Land and from it to the whole world. For in the Land of Israel the kingship of God, His Torah and His blessing are revealed, and from it they spread to the whole world, whereas outside the Land it is difficult to reveal them. Therefore in the Land it is revealed that the Lord is God, whereas outside the Land He is called only "God of gods." Therefore the Sages said that a Jew who lives outside the Land is like one who worships idols (Ketubot 110b). They also said: "As long as you are in the Land, I am your God; when you are not in the Land, it is as if I am not your God" (Tosefta Avoda Zara 4:5). Therefore they said that the mitzva of settling the Land is equivalent to all the mitzvot (Sifrei Re'eh 80; Ramban, Vayikra 18:25).

It is also stated: "For you are crossing the Jordan to come and possess the land that the Lord your God is giving you, and you shall possess it and dwell in it. And you shall be careful to do all the statutes and the ordinances that I set before you this day. These are the statutes and the ordinances that you shall be careful to do in the land that the Lord, the God of your fathers, has given you to possess, all the days that you live upon the earth" (Devarim 11:32-12:1). This implies that the obligation of the mitzvot applies specifically in the Land. However, on the other hand it is stated (ibid. 11:16-18): "Take heed to yourselves lest your heart be deceived, and you turn aside and serve other gods and bow down to them. And the anger of the Lord will be kindled against you … and you will perish quickly from the good land that the Lord is giving you. [And even so, also when you are in exile] you shall place these words of Mine upon your heart and upon your soul, and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as totafot between your eyes." Thus even in exile there is a mitzva to fulfil the mitzvot. The Sages explained that the mitzvot that are dependent on the Land, that is, those connected to the soil, are to be fulfilled only in the Land, while the mitzvot that are not dependent on the Land must be fulfilled in exile as well, so that we will remember them and know how to fulfil them when we return to the Land. Moreover, through fulfilling them we will be roused to repentance and will merit bringing our redemption closer (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; Kiddushin 1:8; Bavli Kiddushin 37a; Sifrei Ekev 43-44).

These are the mitzvot dependent on the Land: ḥalla, orla, kilayim of seeds, kilayim of the vineyard, ḥadash, leket, shikheḥa, pe'a, peret, olelot, bikkurim, terumot and ma'asrot, reshit ha-gez (the first shearing), shevi'it and yovel. According to many, also the gifts of the foreleg, the cheeks and the maw (below, 15). And although the primary obligation of these mitzvot is in the Land, the obligation of many of them extends to some degree outside the Land as well (as explained in the note). There are also many other communal mitzvot that are dependent on the Land, such as establishing a judicial system, and many more mitzvot that depend on the building of the Temple and its existence, and we will not deal with any of these in this chapter.1

The obligation of all the mitzvot dependent on the Land of Israel depends also on the people of Israel, for the obligation of all of them began only after the people of Israel entered the main part of the Land, that is, the western side of the Jordan, which is the land of the seven Canaanite nations. The Torah obligation of shevi'it and yovel depends on the people dwelling in its Land in the proper manner, each tribe in its inheritance (below, 14). And the Torah obligation of ḥalla, terumot and ma'asrot depends on the majority of the people being in the Land (below, halakhot 2, 10, 11).

sections.title: The Beginning of the Obligation
sections.html:
From the time Israel entered the Land they became obligated in the mitzvot that are incumbent on each individual for himself, and these are: ḥadash, orla, kilayim of seeds and kilayim of the vineyard. The land on which these mitzvot took effect is the land that those who came up from Egypt were commanded to conquer on the western side of the Jordan, as explained in Parashat Mas'ei (Bamidbar 34), and from the moment Israel crossed the Jordan the obligation took effect over all of it, even though in practice they had not yet conquered it. And since even before that they had conquered the eastern side of the Jordan, the obligation extended to it as well. But territories outside the boundary of those who came up from Egypt, even though they are within the borders of the Land of Israel – from the River of Egypt to the river Euphrates – did not become obligated in these mitzvot, as long as they had not been conquered by the people of Israel as a whole.2

In the mitzvot connected to the community, that is, terumot and ma'asrot, which are given by the owners of the fields to the kohanim, the Levites and the poor, and likewise shevi'it and yovel, which include all of Israel, they became obligated only after they had finished conquering the Land and dividing it among the tribes. The conquest lasted seven years, and the division into tribes and inheritances, until every person in Israel received his inheritance, lasted another seven years. It follows that in the fifteenth year after their entry into the Land they began to count years for shemita and yovel and to separate terumot and ma'asrot and to leave the gifts for the poor, and in the twenty-first year they observed the first shemita, and in the sixty-fourth year they observed the first yovel (Sifrei Ekev 41; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:1).3

Until the Temple in Jerusalem was built, they would eat the produce of ma'aser sheni and neta revai near the Mishkan at Shilo (Mishna Zevaḥim 14:4-8), and it was there that they would bring up the bikkurim. So it continued for the 369 years of its existence. After that the Mishkan stood for another 57 years in Nov and Giv'on, and from there they went up to Jerusalem, to the Temple built by Shlomo, which stood for 410 years (Zevaḥim 118b; Rambam, Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 1:2).

sections.title: Syria
sections.html:
Beyond the borders conquered by Moshe and Yehoshua, in which the twelve tribes received their inheritances, King David conquered Syria, including territories within the borders of the Land of Israel such as Aram Damascus, and territories outside the borders of the Land, such as Aram Naharayim between the Euphrates and the Tigris. His conquest was meant to subdue enemies who might threaten Israel in the future, and instead of hostile kingdoms developing there, David stationed governors there who collected tribute from them to strengthen his kingdom (II Shmuel 8:3-13; 10:16-19). The Sages said that this conquest was not carried out in the proper order, since the mitzva was first to conquer the entire land of Canaan within the borders explained in Parashat Mas'ei (Bamidbar 34), and he conquered Syria before he conquered Jerusalem, which was ruled by the Jebusites (Sifrei Ekev 51). Apparently David departed from the order because he did not intend to designate Syria for Jewish settlement, since at that time the people of Israel had not yet properly filled the territories it had inherited in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun. And he held that if he conquered Syria in order to subdue enemies and collect tribute from them to strengthen his kingdom, this is not considered a departure from the proper order. Therefore his conquest is called a "kibush yaḥid" (an individual's conquest), which was carried out to strengthen his kingdom and not in order to settle the Land.

Since the conquest was not in the proper order, a doubt arose regarding its status. According to Rabbi Meir, although Syria was conquered by an individual's conquest, there is a Torah obligation to fulfil the mitzvot dependent on the Land there. Therefore one is obligated by Torah law to separate terumot and ma'asrot in Syria, and it is forbidden to sell a house there to a gentile. According to Rabbi Yosei, since it was conquered by an individual's conquest, it became obligated in the mitzvot dependent on the Land only by rabbinic law, including the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot, and in a time of need it is permitted to sell a house there to a gentile. And so the halakha was ruled (Gittin 8a-b; Avoda Zara 21a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 10:3). However, even according to Rabbi Yosei, since all the territories up to the river Euphrates are within the borders of the Land of Israel, there is a mitzva to settle them and to buy houses in them, and even on Shabbat a Jew is permitted to transgress a rabbinic prohibition of "shevut" in order to buy a house there (Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 6:11).4

sections.title: The Days of Exile and the First Destruction
sections.html:
From the time the members of the tribes of Re'uven, Gad and half of Menashe were exiled (in the year 3188 from the creation of the world), about a hundred and fifty years before the destruction, the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel lapsed by Torah law, as it is stated (Vayikra 25:10): "And you shall proclaim liberty in the land to all its inhabitants" – "at a time when all its inhabitants are upon it, and not at a time when some of them have been exiled"; and when the obligation of yovel lapses, the obligation of shevi'it lapses as well (Arakhin 32b; Gittin 36a. The reason is explained in Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 1:9; 5:3).

They were still obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law, and although they observed the mitzva of shevi'it by rabbinic law or by custom, the counting of the shemita years, on which the obligation of the tithes depended, continued by Torah law (see Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 10:5; and see Tosafot, Arakhin 12b, s.v. "hanakh shnei").

About eighteen years later (in the year 3206 from the creation of the world), the Torah obligation of ḥalla and of terumot and ma'asrot lapsed, since the majority of Israel was no longer in its Land. And from the time the First Temple was destroyed, the sanctity that forms the basis for the obligation of all the mitzvot fulfilled by the community lapsed, such as ḥalla and teruma, which are given to the kohanim; ma'aser rishon, which is given to the Levites; ma'aser sheni, which all of Israel eats in Jerusalem; ma'aser ani, which is given to the poor; and shevi'it and yovel, which depend on all the tribes of Israel being in their inheritances. For since these mitzvot depend on the situation of the people of Israel as a whole, the foundation of their obligation lapsed at the time of the destruction. This is what the Sages said (Ḥullin 7a): "The first sanctity sanctified for its time but did not sanctify for the future," meaning that the first sanctity lapsed with the destruction of the First Temple.

But in the mitzvot fulfilled by each individual for himself, such as orla and kilayim, one is obligated by Torah law even after the destruction of the Temple and the exile of Israel. For since their obligation began from the time they entered the Land, even before they conquered it and divided its inheritances, the destruction and the exile do not cancel their obligation.5

sections.title: The Prophets' Enactment of Terumot and Ma'asrot in Babylonia
sections.html:
At the end of the days of the First Temple, after the exile of Yehoyakhin, when a community of exiles began to form in Babylonia, the prophets instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated also from the produce that grows in Shin'ar, which is Babylonia, because it is adjacent to the Land of Israel and many Jews would go and settle there. The enactment was meant to preserve the values of the mitzva among the exiles and to help the poor. And perhaps they were also concerned that there would be Jews who would prefer to leave the Land in order to be exempt from the obligation to separate twenty percent of the crop for terumot and ma'asrot; therefore they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in Babylonia as well. And since there is no mitzva of shevi'it in Babylonia, they instituted that in shevi'it too terumot and ma'asrot be separated, and that "ma'aser sheni" be separated (as will be explained below, 13).

Apparently they continued to separate terumot and ma'asrot in Babylonia even after the destruction of the Temple, and they continued counting the shemita cycles, since it is the basis for the order of separating terumot and ma'asrot, for in years 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7 they separated "ma'aser sheni," and in years 3 and 6 "ma'aser ani" (see Rambam, Hilkhot Shemita Ve-yovel 10:5). However, in the Land the obligation lapsed, and presumably there were those who separated terumot and ma'asrot as a matter of custom, but they were not obligated to do so, until the Men of the Great Assembly returned and sanctified the Land a second time.

Even after the Land was restored and sanctified a second time, the enactment of the prophets remained in place. And the elders who led Israel after Ezra the Scribe further instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in Egypt as well, since there too there was a large Jewish community. Except that they instituted that in shevi'it "ma'aser ani" be separated in Egypt, so that the poor of the Land could be helped by it during shevi'it. Afterwards they likewise instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in the lands of Amon and Moav, and it was ruled that in shevi'it "ma'aser ani" be separated (Mishna Yadayim 4:3).6

sections.title: Accepting the Torah in the Days of Ezra
sections.html:
Fifty-two years after the destruction of the First Temple, Koresh king of Persia gave permission to the Jews of Babylonia to return to the Land and build the Temple. But only 42 thousand volunteered and went up to the Land. The returnees settled in Jerusalem and its surroundings, built the altar and offered sacrifices on it, and prepared to build the Temple. However, following letters of accusation that the gentiles of the land sent to the Persian kingdom, the building of the Temple was halted for 18 years, until Daryavesh II, the son of Aḥashverosh and Queen Esther, permitted the building of the Temple (Megilla 11b-12a, and Rashi there).

However, the national and spiritual situation of the people of Israel was still at a low ebb. The overwhelming majority of the people preferred to remain in exile, and the Jewish community in the Land was small in number and poor in spirit. Few engaged in Torah study, many mitzvot were neglected, and even among the sons of the kohanim many sinned and married foreign women. They apparently thought that in the new reality, in which the people of Israel was scattered and dispersed among the nations, there was no longer an obligation to observe the mitzvot. It was then clear that, in view of the new era, it was necessary to establish how the Torah would continue to be fulfilled in Israel.

In the sixth year after the building of the Temple, the spiritual giant Ezra the Scribe came up from Babylonia and began to rouse the people to engage in Torah and to fulfil the mitzvot. Regarding Ezra's greatness the Sages said (Sanhedrin 21b): "Ezra was worthy that the Torah be given through him, had Moshe not preceded him." They also said (Sukka 20a): "When the Torah was forgotten from Israel, Ezra came up from Babylonia and re-established it." In addition to being a sage he was also a prophet, and his prophetic name was Malakhi (Megilla 15a). About 13 years after Ezra's ascent, the official Neḥemya came up to Jerusalem, holding governmental authority from the king of Persia, and together with Ezra he established the Jewish community in the Land both nationally and religiously.

The Sages said that the coming of Israel to the Land in the days of Ezra the Scribe is compared to their coming in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun: just as in their coming in the days of Yehoshua they accepted the mitzvot upon themselves, so too in their coming in the days of Ezra. And just as those who came up from Egypt were commanded that after their entry into the Land, at the assembly at Mount Gerizim and Mount Eival, they should again make a covenant on the Torah they had received at Sinai (Devarim 11:29-32; 27:1-26), so too they had to make a covenant on it again in the days of Ezra (Yerushalmi Shevi'it 6:1; Bavli Arakhin 32b).

And so indeed it is related in Scripture that in the days of Ezra and Neḥemya, Israel accepted upon themselves to observe the Torah, emphasizing the mitzvot that needed strengthening. As it is stated (Neḥemya 10:1-40): "And because of all this we make a firm covenant and write it, and on the sealed document are our princes, our Levites and our priests. And on the sealed documents (the fathers' houses of the kohanim and the Levites, and the heads of the people) … and they enter into a curse and into an oath to walk in God's Torah, which was given by Moshe the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our Lord, and His ordinances and His statutes; and that we will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land (the gentiles), nor take their daughters for our sons; and if the peoples of the land bring wares or any grain on the Sabbath day to sell, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on a holy day (not to trade on Shabbat and festivals); and that we will forgo the seventh year (to rest in shevi'it), and the exaction of every debt (the remission of debts) … and to bring the first fruits of our ground and the first fruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of the Lord; and the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as it is written in the Torah, and the firstlings of our herds and of our flocks, to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God; and that we should bring the first of our dough (ḥalla) and our terumot, and the fruit of every tree, wine and oil, to the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God, and the tithes of our ground to the Levites …"

In order to establish the Torah in Israel, Ezra the Scribe founded the great beit din, the most important in the history of Israel, which was called the "Great Assembly," and in it were members one hundred and twenty sages, among them the last of the prophets. This beit din examined the state of Judaism and established enactments through which the people of Israel would be able to survive even while dispersed, part of it in the Land and most of it outside the Land. Among other things, the Men of the Great Assembly instituted the text of the prayers and blessings, the times of the Torah reading in the synagogues, and the times at which the courts would sit to judge between man and his fellow. Through these enactments the Men of the Great Assembly restored the Torah in Israel and laid the foundation for the continued building of the Oral Torah, by raising up many students, and by paving the way for the sages of Israel in the coming generations to enact enactments and establish safeguards according to the needs of the generation.7

sections.title: The Second Sanctity and Its Force for the Communal Mitzvot
sections.html:
One of the harshest expressions of the crisis that befell the people of Israel following the destruction of the First Temple was the cancellation of the obligation to fulfil the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, such as shemita and yovel, terumot and ma'asrot and the gifts for the poor – the mitzvot through which the divine values find expression in practical public life, and through which the unique character of the people of Israel is revealed. Presumably, even after the destruction there were still Jews who continued to fulfil these mitzvot to some extent. But they did so as an ancestral custom and not because they were obligated in them. The crowning achievement of the work of Ezra the Scribe was restoring these mitzvot to their force. In the seventh year after the establishment of the Temple, Ezra and his beit din again sanctified the Land for its mitzvot, and began to count years for shemita and yovel, and Israel again became obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, ḥalla, the gifts for the poor and shevi'it.

The Sages said that the first sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified for the communal mitzvot in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun, was sanctified for its time and lapsed at the time of the destruction. But the second sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified in the days of Ezra, remained forever. For it is stated in the Torah that after we sin and the punishment of exile is fulfilled in us, God will bring us back to our Land a second time, as it is stated (Devarim 30:3-5): "Then the Lord your God will bring back your captivity and have compassion on you, and will return and gather you from all the peoples where the Lord your God has scattered you … And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it …" The Sages said: "which [your fathers] possessed" – this is the first coming, in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun; "and you shall possess it" – this is the second coming, in the days of Ezra. And since the Torah does not mention that there will be a further possession, it follows that by force of the second possession the Land will remain sanctified forever, and even after the destruction of the Second Temple it will not lapse (Yevamot 82b). For the first sanctity lapsed because it was effected through conquest, and therefore when the Land was taken from us and the conquest ended, the sanctity lapsed. But the second sanctity was effected through Israel settling in the Land and holding on to it despite all the difficulties. And since the sanctity took effect through settlement even though Israel did not have sovereignty, it is based on the claim of right of the people of Israel to its Land, which rests on the divine promise, and since the claim of right never lapses, the destruction and the exile too did not cancel the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot (based on Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:5; Hilkhot Beit Ha-beḥira 6:16). It seems that the first sanctity was the basis for the second sanctity, since the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot is actualized in its fullness through the mitzva of settling the Land in both its parts, conquest and settlement, as it is stated (Devarim 11:31): "and you shall possess it and dwell in it" – possession is conquest, and dwelling is settlement. And after the people of Israel acquired its Land through both parts of the mitzva, the Land remained sanctified for its mitzvot forever.

Admittedly, there are Rishonim who disagree and hold that the second sanctity also lapsed after the destruction (Rashba, Ritva and Ran), but it is accepted in halakha that the second sanctity never lapses.8

sections.title: The Area of the Sanctity: Those Who Came Up from Babylonia and Those Who Came Up from Egypt
sections.html:
Since the second sanctity was established through settlement, it took effect on all the places in which Israel settled in the days of the Second Temple. As the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia expanded, so the boundary of the sanctity expanded, and these places are called the "boundary of those who came up from Babylonia." At first they settled in Yehuda and Binyamin, and over time, thanks to the Hasmonean kingdom, the continuing aliya and natural growth, the settlement expanded to Shomron, to the Lower and Upper Galilee, to the coastal plain from Ashkelon to Akko, to the Golan and to the eastern side of the Jordan.

When they sanctified the area of settlement, the sanctity was reawakened also in all the places that those who came up from Egypt had conquered on both sides of the Jordan, and it even spread to Syria, except that they determined that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the sanctity would take effect by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria by rabbinic law. The Men of the Great Assembly could have determined that the sanctity would spread in full throughout the boundary of "those who came up from Egypt" and Syria, but they chose to leave the places that were not properly settled with a less severe obligation, in order to ease things somewhat for the poor. On the other hand, they could have determined that the sanctity would not apply at all to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and to Syria, but they did not want to exempt them, so that there too the poor could benefit from terumot and ma'asrot and from the renunciation of produce in shevi'it. And even within the area of those who came up from Babylonia there were cities in which gentiles lived, such as Beit She'an and Ashkelon, and the Sages did not apply to them the full obligation of the mitzvot as in the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia (Ḥagiga 3b; Ḥullin 7a). In those days the law of the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and of those cities was known, but in time it was forgotten, and the poskim disagreed about it, as explained below (halakha 12).

In any case, after the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land for the communal mitzvot dependent on it, they no longer needed to sanctify again the places to which Jewish settlement spread in the days of the Second Temple; rather, the sanctity spread together with the settlement. And even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the sanctity remained throughout the area of those who came up from Babylonia, because a place that has already been sanctified with the second sanctity never again loses its sanctity. For we have learned (above, 7) that the Sages expounded that after the second sanctity, with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, Israel will never again need to sanctify it. It follows, then, that what we said, that in the boundary of those who came up from Egypt the obligation of the communal mitzvot is rabbinic, refers to places in which there was no organized Jewish settlement during the days of the Second Temple.9

sections.title: The Decree of Impurity on the Land of the Nations
sections.html:
In the days of the Second Temple the Sages decreed impurity on the "land of the nations," that is, on the places outside the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia in which there was no Jewish settlement. The reason for the decree was that the gentiles would bury their dead in the ground without a grave, and sometimes the bones of their dead would become scattered, broken and mixed with the earth until it was difficult to distinguish them. And the halakha is that a bone of a corpse, whether of a Jew or of a gentile, even the size of a barley grain, renders one who touches it impure. Therefore they decreed that anyone who touches the earth of the land of the nations is considered as having touched a corpse and becomes impure.

An additional reason accompanied the decree: to prevent Israel from leaving the boundary of settlement, in which the essential fulfilment of the mitzva of settling the Land takes place. For this was the aim – that the second sanctity spread gradually with continuous Jewish settlement, and not that Jews scatter among the gentiles without the Land being considered theirs. And indeed we find that this decree was effective, and thanks to it they refrained from leaving the area of Jewish settlement even for a short time. Not only that, but they even called the places outside the area of Jewish settlement "outside the Land" and "the land of the nations," even though they are in the Land of Israel (Gittin 76b).10

Since kohanim are forbidden to become impure through a corpse, after the decree of impurity on the land of the nations, kohanim were forbidden to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. Only when they had a great need, such as to save property, to marry a wife or to study Torah, were they permitted to leave (Avoda Zara 13a). Today, when purity is not practised, kohanim are permitted to leave the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia, and what remains is the general prohibition on every Jew to leave the Land of Israel for outside the Land.11

sections.title: Ḥalla
sections.html:
The mitzva of ḥalla applies in the Land of Israel when the majority of Israel is in the Land, as it is stated (Bamidbar 15:18-19): "When you come into the land to which I bring you, then it shall be, when you eat of the bread of the land, that you shall set apart a teruma (gift) to the Lord." The Sages learned (Ketubot 25a): "'When you come' – I spoke of the coming of all of you, and not the coming of some of you." Therefore, when Israel came up to the Land in the days of Ezra, they were not obligated in the mitzva, since only some of them came up to the Land. However, the Men of the Great Assembly, headed by Ezra the Scribe, instituted that even when the majority of Israel is not in the Land, ḥalla is to be separated (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:5).

Not only that, but the Sages further instituted that ḥalla be separated throughout the world as well, so that the laws of ḥalla would not be forgotten from Israel (Bekhorot 27a; Rambam, ibid. 5:7). They instituted this for ḥalla and not for terumot and ma'asrot because the mitzva of ḥalla is similar to the mitzvot that depend on the person and not on the soil, since one becomes obligated in it at the time of kneading (Tosafot, Kiddushin 36b). Moreover, the mitzva of ḥalla pertains to everyone, whereas the mitzva of terumot and ma'asrot pertains only to farmers (Mahari Kurkus, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:7).

After the Sages decreed impurity on the land of the nations, that is, on all the territories outside the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia, it was no longer possible to eat the ḥalla in all the impure places, since the ḥalla is holy and must be eaten in purity. Therefore the Sages instituted that in the Land of Israel within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt two ḥallot be separated: one ḥalla of the measure the Sages fixed, one forty-eighth, and this is to be burned since it is impure, and through this people will remember that the ḥalla is holy and it is forbidden to eat it in impurity. And another ḥalla is to be separated, of whatever amount the owner of the dough wishes, even a minimal amount, and this is to be given to a kohen, so that people will remember the purpose of the ḥalla, which is meant to be eaten by the kohanim. The kohanim may eat it in impurity, provided they are not impure with an impurity that issues from the body, such as a seminal emission or nidda; and if they became impure through these, after they immerse for their purification they may eat this ḥalla.

In Syria and in all the other lands of the world, where the basis of the obligation of ḥalla is at a lower level, the law is different. When there is a kohen there who is not impure with an impurity that issues from his body, such as a minor who has not yet become impure at all, or an adult who has immersed, one ḥalla is separated and he eats it. When there is no kohen there who is pure of impurity that issues from his body, two ḥallot are separated: one is to be burned, so as to remember that it is forbidden to eat ḥalla in impurity, and for this ḥalla one may separate even a minimal amount. The second may be eaten even by kohanim who are impure with impurity that issues from the body, and its measure is one forty-eighth (Mishna Ḥalla 4:8; Bekhorot 27a; Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 5:7-11).12

Since purity ceased from Israel, kohanim cannot eat ḥalla in the Land of Israel, and therefore in the Land one ḥalla of a minimal amount is separated, and the ḥalla is burned. Some say that this is the practice outside the Land as well, since the basis of the enactment to separate two ḥallot outside the Land was so that people would remember the mitzva of eating the ḥalla that the kohanim eat in the Land; and when ḥalla is not eaten in the Land, outside the Land too there is no room to separate an additional ḥalla for eating, but only one ḥalla for burning, as in the Land of Israel. And this is the prevalent custom (above, 11:4, note 2).

sections.title: Terumot and Ma'asrot: By Torah Law or by Rabbinic Law
sections.html:
It is agreed that the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land a second time, so that Israel would again become obligated in fulfilling the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, including terumot and ma'asrot.

However, the Amora'im and the Rishonim disagreed whether through this we became obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law or by rabbinic law. According to many Rishonim, from the time the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, they became obligated in the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot by Torah law. And regarding the period after the Temple was destroyed they disagreed: some say that the obligation still remains in place, because the Land was sanctified forever (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ). And some say that after the Temple was destroyed, the obligation became rabbinic (Rashba, Ritva, Ran and Sefer Ha-teruma).

According to Rambam, even after the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, the obligation of the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot was rabbinic, because the obligation of the mitzvot of terumot and ma'asrot, like the mitzva of ḥalla, applies by Torah law only when the majority of Israel dwells in its Land. Nevertheless, the sanctity with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land was effective with regard to the very obligation to fulfil the mitzva. And this obligation determines that when the majority of Israel is not in the Land, the obligation is rabbinic, and when the majority of Israel dwells in the Land, they will be obligated by Torah law without any need to sanctify the Land again. And so the later poskim wrote, that the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot in our time is rabbinic, and when the majority of Israel is in the Land, the obligation will be by Torah law.13

sections.title: The Other Places with Respect to Terumot and Ma'asrot
sections.html:
As we have learned (in halakha 8), when the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land, they sanctified the area of settlement, that is, the area of "those who came up from Babylonia," and through this the sanctity was reawakened also in all the places that those who came up from Egypt had conquered on both sides of the Jordan, and it even spread to Syria. And the Sages determined that by force of that sanctity all the places would be obligated to fulfil the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land, except that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the foundation of the obligation of the mitzvot is by Torah law, and within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria it is by rabbinic law. In later times Yoḥanan the High Priest instituted the enactment of "demai," according to which one must separate, out of doubt, ma'asrot and terumat ma'aser from produce bought from amei ha-aretz (people not reliable regarding tithes), and he determined that this enactment would apply to the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and not to the boundary of those who came up from Egypt. This is the only difference in the law of terumot and ma'asrot between the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia and the boundary of those who came up from Egypt according to most Rishonim, and so the Aḥaronim ruled.

However, some Rishonim hold that the difference between them is greater: that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia one must separate terumot and ma'asrot from all fruits and vegetables, according to the enactment of the Sages, whereas within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt one must separate only from grain, wine and oil, whose obligation is by Torah law (Rashi, Ra'avad and Kaftor Va-feraḥ).14

In Syria it is agreed that by the basic law one must separate terumot and ma'asrot, but many were accustomed not to separate, because they held that even lands bought by Jews actually belonged to the king, and land of a gentile in Syria is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot even when a Jew completed the work of gathering the produce (Gittin 47a; above, end of note 4). However, in practice the poskim wrote that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot in Syria from land registered in the name of a Jew.15

sections.title: Terumot and Ma'asrot Outside the Land
sections.html:
As we have learned (in halakha 5), the prophets and the Sages instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in four lands adjacent to the Land: Babylonia, Egypt, Amon and Moav. And even after the Sages decreed impurity on the land of the nations, the Sages determined that the kohanim may eat the terumot there, on condition that they are not impure with an impurity that issues from the body (above, 10). They were not permitted to bring the produce of "ma'aser sheni" up to Jerusalem; rather, they would redeem it for money in order to buy food with it in Jerusalem (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14). And since the mitzva of shemita does not apply outside the Land, they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in shevi'it as well.

In practice, already in the period of the Ge'onim it was not the custom to separate terumot and ma'asrot in the four lands adjacent to the Land, and the Ge'onim explained that since the practice of purity ceased in Israel, the enactment to separate terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land lapsed. Admittedly, in Rambam and the Shulḥan Arukh it is ruled that one must separate terumot and ma'asrot in those four lands, and some say that this is the proper practice ideally. However, in practice the custom is not to separate terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land at all.16

sections.title: Shevi'it
sections.html:
Nearly all the Tanna'im agree that about a hundred and fifty years before the destruction of the First Temple, when the king of Assyria exiled the members of the tribes of Re'uven, Gad and half of Menashe, the Torah obligation of the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel lapsed. For only when Israel dwells in its Land in the proper manner, the majority of each tribe in its inheritance, is one obligated in the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel by Torah law (Arakhin 32b; Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:4, note 3). It follows, then, that the sanctity with which the Men of the Great Assembly sanctified the Land with respect to the mitzvot of shevi'it and yovel established that although in the days of the Second Temple they were not obligated to fulfil them by Torah law, they would be obligated to fulfil them by rabbinic enactment. Furthermore, the sanctity with which they sanctified the Land is effective for the time when Israel returns to its Land, each tribe to its inheritance, so that the obligation of shevi'it and yovel will again apply by Torah law without any need to sanctify the Land again.

Even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the rabbinic obligation to observe shevi'it did not lapse. Admittedly, a doubt arose as to when the seventh year is, and in addition some Rishonim hold that from the time the beit din that sanctified months and counted years ceased from Israel, about three hundred years after the destruction of the Second Temple, the obligation to rest in shevi'it lapsed, and it is good to observe shevi'it in our time only as a custom of piety (Razah and Ra'avad). However, in practice the view of the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim is that even today one must observe shevi'it by rabbinic law, according to the count accepted among us (Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 5:6-7, notes 5-6).

In the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria too, one is obligated to rest in shevi'it, except that within the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia the Sages decreed not to eat sefiḥim, that is, vegetables that grow by themselves, whereas within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria they did not decree this (Rambam, Semag, Ḥinukh and others). Some are lenient and hold that within the boundary of those who came up from Egypt and in Syria it is even permitted to eat the produce of shevi'it after the time of bi'ur (removal). And some say that their produce does not even have sanctity.17

sections.title: Gifts for the Poor
sections.html:
The mitzvot of leket, shikheḥa, pe'a, peret and olelot, which are left for the poor in the fields, apply by Torah law in the Land of Israel only. And just as they instituted that terumot and ma'asrot be separated in the lands close to the Land of Israel, so they instituted regarding the gifts for the poor throughout the lands outside the Land (Rambam; Tur 332:1), and some say that they instituted this only for the lands adjacent to the Land (Ha-ittur; Shakh, 2).

Although the enactment of giving terumot and ma'asrot outside the Land lapsed in the period of the Ge'onim, the enactment of the gifts for the poor did not lapse. This is because the terumot and "ma'aser sheni" depend on the observance of purity and the Temple service, and therefore we fulfil them in the Land of Israel after the destruction only because of the obligation of the mitzva, without their serving the purposes for which they were established; but outside the Land there is no reason to continue the enactment when it serves no purpose. The gifts for the poor, however, were of benefit to the Jewish poor outside the Land as well, and therefore even after the destruction of the Temple the enactment to leave them the gifts remained in place. However, today it is not the custom to leave gifts for the poor, since it is not worthwhile for the poor to take them (as explained above, 6:9).

The poskim disagreed regarding the force of the obligation of the gifts for the poor in the Land of Israel in our time. Their disagreement depends on the question of whether this mitzva is considered an individual mitzva or a communal one, as explained above (halakha 4, and end of note 2). Some say that the mitzva is rabbinic only (Ḥinukh 216; Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 4:39). And some say it is by Torah law (Minḥat Ḥinukh 216:15; Degel Re'uven, part 2, 28-29), and the Torah obligation applies throughout the boundary of those who came up from Egypt (Yeshu'ot Malko, Terumot 1:26).

sections.title: The Priestly Gifts from Animals
sections.html:
Reshit ha-gez (the first shearing): The Tanna'im disagreed on the question of whether the mitzva of reshit ha-gez applies outside the Land as well, and the halakha was ruled that it does not apply outside the Land, just as terumot and ma'asrot do not apply outside the Land (Ḥullin 136b; SA YD 333:1). Regarding the force of the mitzva of "reshit ha-gez" in the Land of Israel, some say that it is by Torah law, and some say that its obligation is rabbinic, like the law of terumot and ma'asrot.18

The foreleg, the cheeks and the maw: According to all the poskim, in all the territories under the rule of the State of Israel one is obligated by Torah law to give them.

However, regarding the obligation of the mitzva outside the Land they disagreed. According to many poskim the mitzva of giving them is equivalent to the mitzvot of reshit ha-gez and terumot and ma'asrot, and consequently one is not obligated to separate them outside the Land (Rashi, Tosafot, Ha-ma'or, Rashba). And some say that only from the mitzva of reshit ha-gez, which was equated with terumot and ma'asrot, is one exempt outside the Land, but in the other gifts from animals one is obligated, since the animal does not grow from the ground, and all the mitzvot pertaining to it apply outside the Land as well (Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 9:1). In practice, the custom outside the Land is not to give the gifts to a kohen (SA 61:21), and some who are meticulous have been accustomed to give them.19

sections.title: The State of Israel Today
sections.html:
The status of all the territories under the control of the State of Israel is like the status of the area of those who came up from Babylonia, in which the foundation of the obligation of all the communal mitzvot dependent on the Land applies by Torah law. And also the territories within the area of those who came up from Egypt, the foundation of whose obligation in the days of the Second Temple was rabbinic – if they are under Israeli control, the foundation of their obligation is by Torah law, like the law of the boundary of those who came up from Babylonia. For we have learned that the second sanctity, with which the Land was sanctified in the days of Ezra, sanctified the Land for all generations, as it is stated (Devarim 30:5): "And the Lord your God will bring you into the land which your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it …" The Sages said: they have a first and a second possession, but not a third. That is, they would need to sanctify the Land the first time in the days of Yehoshua, and the second time in the days of Ezra, but not a third time. From this they learned that even after the destruction of the Second Temple, the sanctity of the Land for its mitzvot did not lapse (Yevamot 82b; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 1:5; above, 7). And although at the time of the Second Temple only the area in which those who came up from Babylonia settled was sanctified by Torah law, since we have learned that there is no further third sanctity, it follows that when the boundary of Jewish settlement expands, the sanctity too expands with it. Just as it was at the time of the Second Temple, when at first only the area around Jerusalem was sanctified, since only there was there Jewish settlement, and as the settlement expanded the sanctity too spread with it. And even after the destruction of the Temple, the sanctity did not depart from the boundary of settlement of those who came up from Babylonia. So too in our days, the sanctity that determines the obligation of the mitzvot dependent on the Land applies to all the places under Israeli rule.

And even according to those who hold that the second sanctity lapsed with the destruction of the Second Temple, the sovereignty of the State of Israel, in the name of the people of Israel as a whole, over the territories of the Land of Israel brings upon them the sanctity that determines the Torah obligation of the mitzvot. As Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Terumot 1:2): "The Land of Israel mentioned everywhere refers to the lands that a king of Israel, or a judge, or a prophet conquers with the consent of the majority of Israel, and this is what is called a conquest of the many." And he further wrote (Hilkhot Melakhim 5:6): "All the lands that Israel conquers with a king by authority of the beit din – this is a conquest of the many, and it is like the Land of Israel that Yehoshua conquered in every respect." And our master Rav Kook ztz"l ruled (Mishpat Kohen 144) that when there is no king, the authority of the king passes to the nation as a whole, and whatever is done in the name of the people of Israel has full force. And the Jews who live in the Land are the ones who represent the nation (Horayot 3a).20

Therefore, all the territories under the rule of the State of Israel are obligated in terumot and ma'asrot with a blessing, and one may separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce grown in one place for produce grown in another place. However, it is not proper to separate from produce grown in territories under the rule of other states for produce grown in the State of Israel, or vice versa, because some hold that in the territories under Israeli rule the foundation of the mitzva is by Torah law, and in the territories outside the borders of the State the foundation of the mitzva is rabbinic.

When the majority of Israel dwells in the Land, according to all views the obligation of terumot and ma'asrot will be by Torah law in all the territories under Israeli rule (see Peninei Halakha: Shevi'it and Yovel 11:3-4, on the number of Jews in the world).21
